args.text: [lane-plover] Risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to servers that have moved or been retired, causing outages or errors. (2) Slow failover: when a service switches to a backup address, clients keep using the dead one until the cached answer expires. (3) Lingering bad data: a poisoned or hijacked answer stays in the cache and keeps misdirecting users long after the source is fixed.

[lane-plover] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so the sender must be able to try again safely. If repeating the request gives the same result as doing it once, a retry cannot cause double charges, duplicate orders or other repeated side effects.

[lane-plover] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a whole-number key, so indexes grow larger and use more memory. (2) Information leak: it begins with a timestamp, so anyone seeing an ID can work out roughly when the row was made, and IDs made in the same millisecond depend on the library for their order.

[lane-plover] A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it alters the main data, so the change is safely stored first. After a crash or power cut, the database replays this log to restore a consistent state, which keeps finished changes and discards half-finished ones.

[lane-plover] (1) Repeatability: a fixed client version means any change in results comes from the system being tested, not from a new client with different defaults or optimisations. (2) Fair comparison: results gathered months apart, or by different people, stay comparable, so a gain or loss cannot be blamed on a client upgrade.

[lane-plover] Backpressure is a way for a full or slow queue to signal the senders to slow down, pause or be refused, rather than letting work pile up without limit. This protects the system from running out of memory and keeps delays predictable, because the pace of incoming work is matched to the pace at which it can be handled.

[lane-plover] Two ways a scheduled job can run twice: (1) a run takes longer than the gap between runs, so the next one starts while the first is still going; (2) the same schedule exists on more than one machine, for example after a server is copied or an app is run in several copies. One guard: take a lock at the start, such as a file or database lock, so a second run finds it held and exits straight away.

[lane-plover] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item in a store that keeps copies on several machines. It tells every copy that the item was removed on purpose, so a machine that missed the deletion does not bring the old item back. Tombstones are cleared after a set period, once all copies have had time to see them.

[lane-plover] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than properly failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change in between, so simply re-running it gives a different result. (2) The failures depend on timing, order or environment, for example they appear only when tests run in parallel, on a slow machine, or after another test has run first.

[lane-plover] A lease-based lock gives a machine the lock only until a set time, and each machine judges that time using its own clock. If one clock runs fast or slow, the holder may think it still has the lock after the lock service has already given it to someone else, or the service may expire it too early. Two machines then believe they hold the lock at once, which defeats its purpose. Safer designs add a fencing token, a number that rises with each grant, so the protected resource can reject stale holders.
